cruxes.question: Is evaluation (L1) really the lever most worth betting on for the next 5-10 years, or are data, simulation and world models more decisive?
cruxes.why_it_matters: Decides how high D05 ranks, and whether a researcher should bet on evaluation methodology or on the physical-data and modeling line.

sides.label: Evaluation is the top lever
sides.position: Without trustworthy evaluation you cannot tell skill from luck: M3 put 35 points on it, citing SWE-Bench's self-documented contamination; M1 cited the lessons from Alpaca to s1; M7 called evaluation the upstream lever.

sides.label: Data and world models matter more
sides.position: Evaluation only catches errors; it does not create capability: K5 put 35 points on L4, citing deep learning's comeback; K3 said evaluation cannot measure whether a system itself knows it is wrong.

cruxes.evidence_needed: Academic narrow-domain work publicly adopted at scale by leading labs, or third-party validation of world models on long-horizon real-robot tasks.

cruxes.question: Does an academic lab training a narrow foundation model count as real impact only with third-party evaluation (C2), or is a team plus compute (C3 + C4) enough?
cruxes.why_it_matters: Decides whether joining an academic narrow-domain foundation-model project is worth it now, and by which standard to choose such a project.

sides.label: Evaluation is the bar; compute is overrated
sides.position: C6 cited DeepMind choosing games because their evaluation is clean; M4's Web-SSL controlled comparison needed no large compute; M8 said diagnostic work does not depend on compute; M5 deliberately did not select the compute condition, signaling doubt.

sides.label: Team plus compute is the real bar
sides.position: K1 cited the IIT programming club ('nobody was doing it, so I did'): outside adoption is the evidence; K2 cited MapReduce: real demand comes before the platform, no need to wait for evaluation.

cruxes.evidence_needed: Among academic narrow-domain model projects, actual industry adoption rates for projects backed first by third-party evaluation versus projects that built their own.

cruxes.question: World models and spatial intelligence (D08): has the core claim, that predictive representations drive decisions, been validated, or are valuations and narrative running ahead of the evidence?
cruxes.why_it_matters: Decides whether to bet heavily on D08 now or wait for closed-loop real-robot evidence.

sides.label: Bet heavily: the next paradigm
sides.position: C6 said world models are a necessary component of AGI; K1 claimed to have pioneered the category but conceded that 'representations being actually used' is not yet proven; M8 said video foundation models were first to achieve understanding and imagination.

sides.label: Not yet validated; overrated
sides.position: C1 cited AMI Labs' valuation of about $3.5B running ahead of real-robot validation; C5 cited a decade of his own video-prediction work that did not bring deep understanding; M5 said VISTA does not model environment dynamics.

cruxes.evidence_needed: Third-party, reproducible closed-loop results on long-horizon real-robot tasks that separate 'the representation encodes the property' from 'the policy actually uses it to decide'.

cruxes.question: Agent self-improvement (RSI): a real, scarce compounding mechanism now, or compute spend packaged as a narrative?
cruxes.why_it_matters: Decides whether D03 scores a 4 or a 9; the direction with the widest disagreement in this run.

sides.label: Still narrative, packaged compute
sides.position: C4 asked whether RSI is just a synonym for 'spending more compute'; M1 cited METR and Sakana evidence that self-improvement claims are thinly supported so far.

sides.label: Real, scarce, worth a heavy bet
sides.position: K2 cited experience with automated experiment loops and expects ML systems to self-improve by 2027; M3 cited his own Agent Workflow Memory as evidence the mechanism is real.

cruxes.evidence_needed: Compute-normalized, pre-registered multi-round experiments showing sustained real capability gains rather than cherry-picked results.

cruxes.question: Physical AI: bet on abstract world models and representations (D08) as the upstream foundation, or on generative action policies (D07) that can be verified directly?
cruxes.why_it_matters: Affects the ranking of D06, D07 and D08, and whether to learn representation-based planning or action-policy design.

sides.label: D08 is more fundamental: bet on representations
sides.position: C1 said the world model is more fundamental and a policy head is just one implementation; M4 said D08 extends a decade of their own work; M6 said upstream judgment matters more than the action subproblem.

sides.label: Bet on D07: actions are verifiable
sides.position: C2 said the action representation directly decides deployability; M3 said policies that produce actions can be checked right or wrong on control tasks; M7 cited LBM's existing real-robot statistical validation.

cruxes.evidence_needed: Real-robot success rates and sample efficiency for representation-first versus action-first approaches on the same robot tasks.

cruxes.question: Can simulation and synthetic data substitute for scarce real robot data, especially for contact, touch and the long tail?
cruxes.why_it_matters: Decides how D09 ranks, and whether simulation experience is best spent on sim2real as a main line.

sides.label: Yes, a real lever
sides.position: C3 cited saving the company with a simulator when RIVA had six months of cash left, while granting that contact and touch may be overrated; K4 cited MimicGen: a data engine has a far lower entry bar than training a foundation model.

sides.label: No, real data is the core
sides.position: C5 said simulated or generated trajectories create no new information; K3 cited the embodiment-gap lesson from Keen to call synthetic data a big mistake; K5 said simulation is an aid to RL, not a road to understanding.

cruxes.evidence_needed: Whether quantified sim2real success rates in non-deterministic physical settings such as contact and touch can be reproduced by third parties.

cruxes.question: Does RL and post-training (RLVR) teach new reasoning abilities, or polish and resample abilities the model already has?
cruxes.why_it_matters: Decides how D02 ranks, and whether progress in reasoning can come from method rather than pure scale.

sides.label: Teaches real capability
sides.position: C3 said reasoning is a second exponential and small compute can produce landmark work (s1); C4 cited DeepSeek-R1 as proof of a real small-compute contribution; M2 said RL is a capability lever but needs honest evaluation.

sides.label: Mainly polishing and resampling
sides.position: K4 said RLVR mainly resamples existing abilities and introduces no new reasoning patterns; K6 said it looks more like execution getting cheaper than a new paradigm; M6 said RLVR mainly improves sampling efficiency.

cruxes.evidence_needed: Controlled experiments where the RLVR-trained model solves out-of-distribution tasks that the base model cannot reach even with unlimited sampling.

open_questions.question: Is the reliability of evaluators (LLM/VLM-as-judge) getting better or worse?
open_questions.why: A shared premise of the evaluation-related judgments at X1 and X3; if it changes, they must be redone.

open_questions.question: How much of today's AI capex is real demand, and how much is propped up by circular deals?
open_questions.why: Decides how high the window score for scale-up directions such as D14 and D01 should be.

open_questions.question: Do the representations of JEPA-style and video world models hold up in non-deterministic physical settings such as contact and touch?
open_questions.why: Decides whether to bet heavily on D06 and D08 now.

open_questions.question: Once evaluation and continual learning, the two current counterexamples, are commoditized, what is academia's next unabsorbed niche in agents?
open_questions.why: Decides whether a direction chosen now still stands in three to five years.

open_questions.question: In the cost of reported agent 'self-improvement', how much is methodological progress and how much is brute-force compute trial and error?
open_questions.why: Decides which end of the 4-to-9 range D03 should land in.
